lab.title: Lab
lab.subtitle: Nine studies. Here the scrollbar is not navigation — it is the playhead.
lab.reducedMotion: Your system asks for reduced motion, so this renders its final state directly.

scrollVideo.name: Scroll as playhead
scrollVideo.summary: Not one video tag on the page. Every frame is an image; scroll far enough and it draws that frame.
scrollVideo.note: A 90-frame sequence with scroll progress mapped to a frame number. Scrolling back just draws backwards — there is no reverse-playback stutter.
scrollVideo.captionOneBody: Scroll progress becomes a frame number; the canvas only paints that frame.
scrollVideo.captionTwoBody: With no playback timeline, scrolling up simply draws in reverse.

dissolve.name: Dissolve
dissolve.summary: An image eaten away by a scalar field and a threshold, so the front breaks into organic clumps instead of a straight edge.
dissolve.note: A vertical gradient leads, low-frequency fbm crumbles the edge, high-frequency speckle adds grain. The threshold sweeps the screen as you scroll. This study is now the cover of the portfolio.
dissolve.headline: An edge is not a line
dissolve.body: The dissolve front is driven by a noise field, so it reads like paper wicking water rather than a curtain being drawn.
dissolve.tail: Scroll back and it grows in again.
dissolve.fallback: No WebGL available here, so this falls back to the static composition.

meltingText.name: Melting type
meltingText.summary: Letters congeal into one sticky liquid, then melt down into clean glyphs.
meltingText.note: A gaussian blur bleeds each glyph outward and an alpha threshold pushes anything past 30% opacity back to solid — where two blurred neighbours overlap, they fuse.

grove.name: Grown, not modelled
grove.summary: A moss-covered root with no model file behind it: swept tubes, a cushion that follows the light, ferns and flower sprays, and nearly two hundred thousand instanced blades.
grove.note: Nothing in the scene itself runs on a clock: how far the survey front has travelled, how brightly the cage rides it, how long the moss has grown, when the flowers open and where the butterfly is are all pure functions of scroll position. The pointer is the one live input — the whole composition leans with it, the fur parts under it, a trail of pollen comes up out of the moss where it passes, and coming too close to the perched butterfly startles it into beating its wings. That layer runs only while something is still actually changing: the pollen falls out, the lean comes home, the startle wears off. When all three are done it stops, and a parked scene draws not one frame. This study is now the cover of the home page.
grove.headline: It is grown, not drawn
grove.body: One seed settles the whole landscape: where the root bends, which flank the moss takes, which hollow a fern comes up in, where every single blade stands. Reload and it grows back identical.
grove.tail: Run the pointer through the moss. Scroll back and it un-grows.
grove.fallback: No WebGL available here, so this falls back to the static composition.

groveStage.name: Two sheets of paper, one root apart
groveStage.tagline: DOM over and under a canvas
groveStage.summary: The same moss, two identical paper cards: one painted under the canvas with the root draped over its shoulder, one standing in front of it — at the reference composition's own coordinates.
groveStage.note: A card cannot stand behind a photograph of a grove, only behind a grove that is still being drawn. The whole trick is one rule: card a carries no z-index, so it paints under the canvas and the root crosses its lower right corner; card b sits at z 3. Card a's knob therefore cannot live inside it, and is rendered on its own, riding the moss. The pair stands where the reference composition put it on its 1600 × 880 grid — 890 × 200 and 1237 × 482, corner to corner on one diagonal — and it is the pair that carries the depth: two sheets of the same paper at the same size, one root apart. Split them to opposite corners and each still crosses the moss, but there is nothing left to compare. Under the pointer the two ride by different amounts, and that difference is the distance between them. The home page's approach uses the same coordinates.
groveStage.pointerHint: Move the pointer · each sheet rides its own depth
groveStage.fallback: No WebGL available here, so this is the two cards alone on an empty stage.

liquidMetal.name: A button, computed all the way down
liquidMetal.tagline: A WebGL2 dispersion shader in five passes
liquidMetal.summary: No gradient, no texture, no image behind it. A scalar field is painted through a soft plateau, sampled at a slightly different height for every wavelength — which is where the rainbow edge comes from.
liquidMetal.note: Here the scrollbar is not a timeline but a way through the pipeline: act one is the bare dispersion field, razor-etched; act two pours the softening blur over it and lights the travelling rim; act three adds the bloom and the contrast curve that put the metal back. The button stays live the whole way down — hover it, hold it, tab to it. The clock only turns while you are touching it, or while it is still settling. The two controls on the home page's cover are this button.
liquidMetal.headline: Solved, not drawn
liquidMetal.body: Fringe width falls out as dispersion over the magnitude of the field's gradient. So one shader gives razor-thin rainbow lines where the field is pinched, and broad navy-to-cyan washes where it is not.
liquidMetal.tail: Hold it down. Watch the crease run round the rim as you let go.
liquidMetal.fallback: No WebGL2 available here, so this falls back to the button alone.
liquidMetal.label: Hold it down

workstation.name: A desk you can spin
workstation.summary: The 3D desk left over from the old portfolio: it swings round to face you on entry, its screens breathe, and a drag leaves it coasting on inertia.
workstation.note: The model came in at 8.5 MB and was compressed to 1.1 MB with gltf-transform (Draco + 1024px WebP); the Draco decoder is self-hosted. It loads only once scrolled near, samples at 30 fps while idle and runs flat out during a drag, and skips itself entirely under Save-Data. The wheel only takes over zoom in the band right above the desk — everywhere else the page scrolls as usual.

lensSlider.name: Lens slider
lensSlider.tagline: Three.js shader + a lens for a transition
lensSlider.summary: Four photographs. Turning the page is not a wipe but a lens growing out of the centre of the frame: the next picture sits inside it, pulled hardest at the rim, and only once the circle has swallowed the frame does the distortion let go.
lensSlider.note: The shader takes two pictures and one progress. The circle's radius grows with it; inside, every pixel is pulled toward the centre by an amount that is its closeness to the rim raised to the fifth power, so only a narrow band hugging the edge magnifies and the middle stays flat. Past the half-diagonal the circle covers the frame, and the rest of the progress is that band relaxing. A ring of water ripples runs out from the rim and dies with the same curve — the one thing the original has that the breakdown left out. Each band of the scrollbar opens the lens onto the next picture; scroll back while it is still growing and it shrinks away again. After Oscar Pico's project slider (oscarpico.es), written from TTTISE's breakdown of it.
lensSlider.fallback: No WebGL available here, so this falls back to a plain change of picture.

neon.name: Welcome to fhf's
neon.tagline: SVG lettering traced from the film's sign + a filter for the tube + a GSAP flicker score
neon.summary: A brick wall, a blue neon sign, Mia & Sebastian's Theme, and a few stills on the wall. The sign is drawn stroke by stroke after the one over the door of Seb's in La La Land, with the name swapped for mine.
neon.note: There is no font, on the sign in the film or here: the lettering follows a vector traced stroke by stroke from the film and published on Wikimedia Commons (Seb's.svg, Espandero, CC BY-SA 4.0). The ring's centre and radius, the angles of its two breaks — at the top right where the note's stem leaves it, and at the lower left — the ends of the bar, and the whole outlines of the S and the note are measured straight off it. The original has no F or H: the F is its E without the foot, the stem closed with the same rounded end as the arms, keeping even the little stub of the middle arm that pokes out past the stem; the H is two stems joined by a bar as heavy as the E's middle arm, its edges on the same tilt. The letters stand upright on a baseline that climbs 9.5° to the right; the ring's left arc simply stops at the lower left, while the right arc runs round the bottom and folds back up into the bar — one tube. What is drawn is the solid letter; the tube is found by a filter: feMorphology erodes the shape inward by thirteen units and subtracting that from the original leaves a band of constant width hugging the outline — exactly what a neon shop does, bending tube along the edge of painted lettering. The white core is eroded out of the same band, the halo is the band dilated and blurred, and the four layers merge back into one. The bricks are painted once by a canvas: every brick its own hue and lightness, a hairline of light along its top, a shadow under it, grain over the lot; after that not one frame is painted. Lighting up is not a fade but a fixed score of blinks: the ring stutters first, the bar follows, then the letters one at a time, each hesitating in its own way, until it holds. The sign is the bar's main switch: lights off, music stops; lights on, it plays again and the music comes back. The same sign now hangs over the site's front door: landing on the cover you meet it first, and the way in is through the ring — the letters go dark, the ring holds, the paper shows through it and the wall pushes past you. The music is the site's background music, its player hidden in the layout behind the wall: it runs through Spotify's iFrame API and is asked to play the moment the sign holds steady; if the browser refuses (you have not clicked anything on this site yet), your first click on the page tries again; once inside, the note on the island is its switch. Without a Spotify login it is a 30-second preview, restarted when it ends. Where Spotify cannot be reached at all (the script errors, or says nothing for 12 seconds), the player behind the wall becomes NetEase Cloud Music's own embed of Hurwitz's 2026 tenth-anniversary re-recording: it has no remote, so it can only be mounted and unmounted with the switch, and it makes no sound until you have clicked somewhere on the page. Further along the wall hang a few stills from the film's nights.
